659.title: Before you were a thing
659.hook: was there a time when the human was nothing worth mentioning (76:1)
659.howItsDone: Surah al-Insan (also called ad-Dahr) is recited in some mosques in the dawn prayer on Fridays, alongside as-Sajdah, following the Prophet's practice reported in Bukhari and Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jibril, and your line, don't hurry. Today a new surah, named for us: al-Insan, the Human.

Find a photo from before you were born. Your parents' wedding, maybe, or a family picnic. Everyone's laughing, squinting into the sun. The world is going on, full of people and plans and weather. And you're nowhere. Not hiding, not waiting offstage. Just not yet. Nobody in the picture is thinking of you, because there is no you yet to think of. Surah seventy-six opens by asking us to think about that on purpose, with a question that isn't really a question.

Verse one, in Pickthall's translation: "Hath there come upon man (ever) any period of time in which he was a thing unremembered?" The Arabic phrase at the end is shay'an madhkura: a thing mentioned, a thing worth speaking of. There was a stretch of time, the verse says, when the human wasn't even that. Not a name, not a memory, not a thought in anyone's head. Some commentators point out that the opening word, hal, usually a question, works here more like a statement: indeed, there came such a time. The answer is built into the asking. Then verse two moves fast: We created the human from a drop, mingled, to test him, and We made him hearing, seeing. From nothing worth mentioning, to a drop, to a listener and a watcher. Verse three: We showed him the way, whether he is grateful or ungrateful. The surah has a second name, ad-Dahr, Time, after this first verse. And it has a special place in the week. According to hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would recite it, along with surah as-Sajdah, in the dawn prayer on Fridays, and some mosques keep that custom. There, Friday begins by remembering the human was once nothing. Why start there? Because if you were once not even a thing mentioned, then everything since, your breath, your name, the people in your life, the very ability to hear these words, arrived as a gift. Gratitude starts from zero.

Picture the world a year before you arrived: the same sky, the same streets, maybe your parents young, and you not in it, and stay with that for a few breaths, without fear. Then slowly add yourself back: your first breath, your name said for the first time, your eyes opening, your ears hearing. Notice each one as something that arrived.
Ad-Dahr, Time: the surah's second name, after its opening question about a stretch when the human wasn't even a thing worth mentioning. Today's word.
Your line: once, nothing. Your hands, your hearing, the people near you: none of it was always there. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

660.title: For love of Him
660.hook: they feed the poor, the orphan and the captive, for His sake, wanting no thanks (76:8–9)
660.howItsDone: Feeding the hungry is praised in the Qur'an and hadith; Muslims give food in Ramadan and through the year, and 76:8–9 is cited for giving for Allah's sake alone, without seeking thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ad-Dahr, and your line, once, nothing. Today al-Insan shows what grateful people do with their hands.

A family at sunset, about to eat for the first time all day. The bread is on the table. Then a knock: someone outside is hungry. They hand over the bread. The next evening, another knock, another hungry person, and the bread goes again. And the third night, a third. They go to bed with empty stomachs, three nights running. A story like this is told about a family very close to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and it's linked to a few verses in surah al-Insan.

Verses eight and nine, in Pickthall's translation: "And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him, (Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." Three people at the door: the poor, the orphan, and the captive. Commentators note that in the Prophet's time a captive could be a prisoner of war who was not a Muslim, and the verse praises feeding them too: hunger doesn't check anyone's religion. Now, a puzzle in two words: 'ala hubbihi. Pickthall says for love of Him, meaning Allah. But the Arabic pronoun could also point to the food: they feed others despite loving it, while they want it themselves. Commentators have defended both readings, and some say both are true. Either way, the giving costs something. Then the attitude: we want no reward from you, and no thanks. Not even a thank-you. And the family at the door? Shia Muslims, and a number of Sunni commentators, hold that these verses came down about 'Ali, Fatimah, and their sons Hasan and Husayn, who fasted three days and gave their bread away each night to a poor man, an orphan, and a captive. Shia tradition treats this as firmly established. Other Sunni scholars question the chain of that report, and read the verses as describing the righteous in general. Both read the same verses with deep respect. And in both readings, the people at the door never had to say thank you.
screen: `FOR LOVE OF HIM, OR OF THE FOOD?`

'Ala hubbihi. For love of Him, or despite love of the food: two readings of 76:8–9, where the righteous feed the poor for Allah's sake alone. Today's word.

661.title: Morning and evening
661.hook: remember your Lord's name morning and evening, and prostrate at night (76:25–26)
661.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the adhkar of the morning and evening, short remembrances, verses and prayers, after the dawn prayer and around sunset, often from a small booklet or from memory, following 76:25, 33:42 and many hadith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'ala hubbihi, and your line, no thanks wanted. Today, our last day in al-Insan, and the two hinges of every day.

Every day has two doors. The one you walk out of in the morning, keys in hand, coffee half finished. And the one you walk back through in the evening, shoes off, bag dropped, the day behind you. It's easy to cross both without noticing, already thinking about the next thing. Near the end of surah al-Insan, after its long picture of a garden for the grateful, the Qur'an gives the Prophet a short instruction about those two doors.
screen: `OUT IN THE MORNING, IN AT EVENING.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-five, in Pickthall's translation: "Remember the name of thy Lord at morn and evening." The Arabic is bukratan wa asila. Bukrah is the early morning, the first hours. Asil is late afternoon into evening, as the light goes gold. Then verse twenty-six: and part of the night, prostrate to Him, and glorify Him through a long night. So the day gets framed: begin with His name, end with His name, give some of the dark to prayer. Commentators connect these times to the daily prayers: the dawn prayer, the afternoon and evening prayers, and the night prayer. And surah al-Ahzab uses the same pairing: remember Allah often, and glorify Him morning and evening. From these verses and many hadith grew a practice millions of Muslims keep: the adhkar of the morning and the evening. Short remembrances, said after the dawn prayer and again before or after sunset. Phrases of praise, verses like Ayat al-Kursi and the last three surahs, and a prayer for forgiveness that a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari calls the master of all prayers for forgiveness, to be said morning and evening. Some people say them from a small booklet; some from memory, walking to the bus. Why the two ends of the day? Because those are the hinges. What you say as the door opens sets the tone for whatever comes through it. What you say as it closes is what you carry into sleep. The middle of the day will be busy. The edges can be held.
screen: `BEGIN WITH HIS NAME, END WITH IT.`

662.title: Those sent forth
662.hook: by the winds sent forth one after another (77:1)
662.howItsDone: Al-Mursalat is a short Meccan surah recited in prayer; commentators differ on whether its first verses describe winds, angels or both.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed al-Insan with adhkar, and your line: the edges can be held. Today a new surah, al-Mursalat.

A cave in Mina, outside Mecca. A small group sits with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, one of his companions, later remembered it: a new surah was coming down, and Ibn Mas'ud was taking it fresh from the Prophet's mouth. Then a snake slid out of the rock. The Prophet told them to kill it. They rushed it, and it got away. And he said, more or less: it was spared your harm, as you were spared its harm. That's how al-Mursalat arrived, in a hadith in al-Bukhari. Surah seventy-seven opens with something that keeps coming.

Wal-mursalati 'urfa. By those sent forth, one after another. Al-mursalat comes from the root r-s-l, to send, the same root as rasul, a messenger, and risalah, a message. So the very first word of the surah is about sending. But sent forth what? The verse doesn't name them, and commentators read it in more than one way. Some say the winds, gust after gust. Others say angels, sent down with Allah's commands. Some held both together. 'Urfan has two readings as well: one after another, like the hairs of a horse's mane, also called 'urf, lying in a row; or with kindness, from the same letters as ma'ruf, the good and decent thing. Then five oaths in a run: those sent forth, those that blow hard, those that spread, those that separate, those that bring down a reminder. Five lines that sound like weather rolling in. Verse six says why the reminder comes: as an excuse or a warning. Verse seven lands the point: what you are promised will surely happen. Before the surah says anything about the Day to come, it points at something you've felt on your face. Wind doesn't arrive once. It keeps coming. The One who keeps sending the wind keeps sending reminders too. Umm al-Fadl, the Prophet's aunt by marriage, said in another hadith that al-Mursalat was the last surah she heard him recite, at the sunset prayer, near the end of his life. A surah about things that keep coming, and it kept being recited to the end.

Listen for something that repeats: a fan, traffic, a clock, wind against a window, a neighbor's footsteps, or, if the room is silent, your own breath, coming in again without your asking. Pick one and stay with it, and let each return count as one more arrival.
Al-mursalat. Those sent forth, one after another: angels or winds, the first word of surah seventy-seven, from the root of messenger. Today's word.
Your line: sent forth. Wind, breath and reminders never come just once. Day six hundred sixty-two.

663.title: Woe that day
663.hook: the refrain repeated ten times: woe that day to the deniers (77:15)
663.howItsDone: Al-Mursalat is recited in prayer and in personal reading; its refrain returns ten times, and commentators read each return against the sign that comes just before it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-mursalat, and your line, sent forth. Today, the second half of al-Mursalat, and the last day of this stretch of the book.

Some songs are built on a chorus. The verse changes, the story moves, and then the same line comes back, and by the third time you're waiting for it. Earlier this year, ar-Rahman did that with a question: which of your Lord's favors will you deny? Al-Mursalat does it too, with a shorter line and a heavier one. It comes back ten times in fifty verses, and the whole surah is built around it.

Surah seventy-seven, verse fifteen, in Pickthall's translation: "Woe unto the repudiators on that day!" In Arabic, waylun yawma'idhin lil-mukadhdhibin. Wayl is woe, a cry of ruin. Yawma'idhin, on that day, the Day the surah has been describing. And al-mukadhdhibin comes from the root k-dh-b, to lie. The form here means more than people who doubt: it's people who call a true thing a lie, who look at it and say, that's false. Pickthall's old word, repudiators, catches that: people who disown what's in front of them. Now watch where the refrain falls. It doesn't only follow scenes of the end. Again and again it follows a gift. Did We not create you from a humble fluid, and shape you? Woe that day to the deniers. Did We not make the earth a place that holds the living and the dead, set firm mountains on it, and give you sweet water to drink? Woe that day to the deniers. The warning keeps landing right after something good. Some commentators read it that way: the denial in view isn't only of the Day, but of the gifts that point to it. To be handed water, a body, solid ground, and call the giver a fiction. So the refrain works in two directions: a warning about the end, and a nudge about this afternoon. What good thing in front of you have you been quietly treating as nothing?

Look back over the last day for one good thing you brushed off: a compliment you waved away, a meal someone made that you ate standing up, a morning you woke up healthy and didn't notice. Hold it for a moment without arguing with it, and let it be what it was: a good thing, given.
Al-mukadhdhibin. Woe that day to the deniers, said ten times in al-Mursalat, often right after a gift: water, body, ground. Today's word.
Your line: don't deny it. The refrain keeps falling right after the gifts. That's day six hundred sixty-three.

664.title: Twenty-five named prophets
664.hook: the Qur'an names twenty-five prophets, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ
664.howItsDone: The twenty-five prophets named in the Qur'an are taught as a list in Islamic schooling, and Muslims add "peace be upon him" (alayhi as-salam) after each prophet's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed al-Mursalat with al-mukadhdhibin, and your line: don't deny it. Today a new stretch begins: the whole book in view, gathered by theme.

Since the start of this year, the path has walked the Qur'an surah by surah, from the Opening to the edge of its last part. Now it steps back, holds the book up like a map, and traces the roads that run all the way through it. The first road is people. Open the book and, again and again, someone is there: a man building an ark, a boy in a well, a father on a mountain with his son. Count the prophets the Qur'an names, by the usual reckoning, and you get twenty-five.

The word is nabi, a prophet. Arabic lexicons connect it to naba', news: a nabi is one who receives news from Allah and passes it on. Some link it to a root meaning to be raised up. Beside it stands rasul, a messenger. One explanation scholars give: every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet was sent with a new message or law. Here are the twenty-five names. Adam. Idris. Nuh. Hud. Salih. Ibrahim. Lut. Isma'il. Ishaq. Ya'qub. Yusuf. Ayyub. Shu'ayb. Musa. Harun. Dhul-Kifl. Dawud. Sulayman. Ilyas. Al-Yasa'. Yunus. Zakariyya. Yahya. 'Isa. And Muhammad ﷺ, called the seal of the prophets in surah thirty-three. Eighteen of them appear in one passage of al-An'am, one name after another. Some will sound familiar from the Bible: Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, John, Jesus. Hud and Salih, sent to the Arabian peoples of 'Ad and Thamud, have no counterpart there. And the list isn't the whole family. The Qur'an says plainly that some messengers' stories it has told, and some it has not. A report in Musnad Ahmad puts the number of prophets in the tens of thousands, though scholars debate its chain. The Qur'an also tells believers to say: we make no distinction between any of His messengers. And a hadith in al-Bukhari gives the picture behind today's line: the prophets are brothers with different mothers and one religion. Different times, different peoples, one family.

Starting with Adam, say each prophet's name you can remember, quietly or in your head, one per breath, without worrying about the order or the gaps. When you get stuck, pause on the last name and recall one thing about him: an ark, a well, a staff, a whale. Muslims customarily add peace be upon him after each name; if that's your practice, add it.
Nabi. A prophet, one who brings news from Allah. Twenty-five are named in the Qur'an, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ, and more are left unnamed. Today's word.
Your line: they are one family. Twenty-five named, and many more untold. Day six hundred sixty-four, done.

665.title: The angels
665.hook: Jibril who brings revelation, Mika'il, Israfil, the recorders on each shoulder
665.howItsDone: Muslims count belief in angels among the pillars of faith; at the end of each prayer they turn the head to the right and then the left with the greeting of peace, which some scholars say includes the angels.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nabi, the prophets, and your line, they are one family. Today, the ones who carried the news to them.

Watch the end of a Muslim prayer. After the last sitting, the person praying turns their head to the right and says, peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah. Then to the left, the same words. If they're praying alone in an empty room, they still turn. Who are they greeting? Partly the people beside them, if there are any. And, some scholars say, someone who's always there: the angels. Today, the mala'ikah.

Mala'ikah is the plural; one angel is a malak. Some lexicons link it to a root for sending a message, and surah thirty-five opens by calling the angels messengers, with wings, two, three and four. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says they were created from light. In the hadith of Jibril, also in Sahih Muslim, belief in them is one of the pillars of faith. A few are named. Jibril, Gabriel, brings the revelation down; al-Baqarah, verse ninety-seven, names him as the one who brought it to the heart of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Mika'il, Michael, is named once, in the very next verse. Tradition connects him with rain and provision. Israfil isn't named in the Qur'an at all: the Qur'an speaks of the trumpet that will be blown on the last Day, and the hadith tradition gives the angel of the trumpet the name Israfil. Then the ones closest to daily life. Surah fifty says two receivers sit, one on the right and one on the left, and not a word is spoken without a watcher ready. Surah eighty-two calls them kiraman katibin: noble ones, writing, who know what you do. Some scholars teach that the one on the right records the good, and the one on the left the bad. And a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim says that when someone intends a good deed and doesn't do it, it's still written as one good deed. Intending a bad one and holding back is written as a good deed too. The ones who write, it turns out, are generous with the pen.
screen: `ONE ON THE RIGHT, ONE ON THE LEFT.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and turn your head gently to the right; if you'd like, say the words of the prayer's end, as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah, or let the greeting be silent. Then turn to the left and do the same. Sit with the thought that a good intention counts, even the ones you didn't finish.
Mala'ikah. Angels, messengers of light: Jibril with revelation, Mika'il, Israfil with the trumpet, and the noble writers on the right and left. Today's word.
Your line: the ones who write. Even an unfinished good intention goes in the record. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: you meant to call a sick friend today, and the day ran out. according to the hadith, what do the writers on your right record?
options: nothing, since it didn't happen.
a missed deed.
one good deed, for the intention.
fork.reveal: the hadith says a good intention not carried out is written as one good deed; carried out, it's multiplied.

trapdoor: what you thought: angels are winged figures in paintings.
what it means: mala'ikah are messengers made of light: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and two noble writers beside each person.
what a scholar hears: Mika'il is named only in 2:98; Israfil's name comes from hadith, not the Qur'an; 50:17–18 places the recorders right and left.
recall: those who call a true thing a lie

chat.says: Why do Muslims turn their heads right and left at the end of prayer?
options: To greet those beside them and, some scholars say, the angels always there.
To check that everyone in the row has finished praying too.
To face Mecca from both sides, as the prayer's ending requires.
chat.meaning: The closing greeting, peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah, goes to the people beside you and, some scholars say, to the angels.
